title: Colon: complete clause, then the explanation or example
subtitle: Boundaries · 11 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **11 of the official questions in Boundaries are this one** — 0 Easy, 3 Medium, 8 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The words before the blank form a complete sentence that sets up something general, like 'something far more ___' or 'one thing'.
- The words after it are a noun phrase that names or defines that thing.
- The choices include a colon, a semicolon, a comma plus a new subject, and a period.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Confirm that the part before the blank is a complete sentence.
- 2) Check whether the part after it is a phrase, not a full sentence, that specifies or elaborates what came before.
- 3) If so, use a colon (or a dash).
- A semicolon and a period both need a full clause after them.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You choose a semicolon because it 'looks formal'.
A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and here the second side is only a noun phrase.
The test also offers a comma plus 'it was', which creates a comma splice.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You choose a semicolon because it 'looks formal'.
A semicolon needs an independent clause on both sides, and here the second side is only a noun phrase.
